prompt: Withdrawal capacity, injection capacity and working gas capacity are given with their prices, together with the gross calorific value. What does it cost to store 12 million m³ of natural gas for one year?
solution:
Storage is billed as three separate reservations, added up (slide "Storage Pricing"):
T_storage = p_injection · κ_injection + p_withdrawal · κ_withdrawal + p_working gas · v_working gas

The trick is always the same: convert volume into energy with the gross calorific value first, because the prices are quoted per kWh.

Worked with the lecture's own figures (GCV = 11 kWh/m³, withdrawal and injection capacity 3,000 m³/h each, working gas 12 million m³; prices 2 €/kWh/h/a withdrawal, 2.5 €/kWh/h/a injection, 0.003 €/kWh/a working gas):

Working gas: 12,000,000 m³ · 11 kWh/m³ = 132,000,000 kWh = 132,000 MWh
 → 132,000,000 kWh · 0.003 €/kWh/a = 396,000 €/a
Withdrawal: 3,000 m³/h · 11 kWh/m³ = 33,000 kWh/h = 33,000 kW
 → 33,000 kW · 2 €/kW/a = 66,000 €/a
Injection: 33,000 kW · 2.5 €/kW/a = 82,500 €/a

Total storage cost = 396,000 + 66,000 + 82,500 = 544,500 €/a

Specific storage cost = 544,500 € / 132,000 MWh = 4.125 €/MWh. That number is the one you need for the follow-up questions.

Note the unit identity that the slides use throughout: €/(kWh/h)/a = €/kW/a — a capacity price, not an energy price.

prompt: Is it profitable to buy natural gas at the summer price, store it and sell it in winter?
solution:
The storage principle slide gives the condition directly: p_supply + p_storage < p_sales. Buying, storing and selling only pays if the summer/winter spread exceeds the specific storage cost.

With the lecture's storage example the specific storage cost is 544,500 € / 132,000 MWh = 4.125 €/MWh. The summer/winter spread slide shows a winter price of 28 €/MWh against a summer price of 27 €/MWh, i.e. a spread of 1 €/MWh.

1 €/MWh < 4.125 €/MWh → the business makes a loss.
Revenue from the spread: 132,000 MWh · 1 €/MWh = 132,000 €
Storage cost: 544,500 €
Result: −412,500 € per year.

That is the point of the slide: the spread alone says nothing. Only spread minus storage cost decides, and in recent years the seasonal spread has often been too thin to pay for a storage booking — which is exactly why the merit order of German storages and the ambiguity of storage prices are discussed right afterwards. A trader who cannot earn the spread will prefer the time swap, which needs no physical capacity.

prompt: How high would the winter selling price have to be for the storage business to break even?
solution:
Rearrange the profitability condition p_supply + p_storage < p_sales to its break-even form:
p_sales = p_supply + p_storage

With the summer price of 27 €/MWh and the specific storage cost of 4.125 €/MWh:
p_sales = 27 + 4.125 = 31.125 €/MWh

The winter price would have to be at least 31.13 €/MWh, i.e. the summer/winter spread would have to reach 4.125 €/MWh instead of the 1 €/MWh shown on the slide. At the actual 28 €/MWh the trader loses 3.125 €/MWh, which over 132,000 MWh is the −412,500 € from the previous part.

General form: the break-even spread equals the specific storage cost, which itself is (p_injection·κ_inj + p_withdrawal·κ_wd + p_working gas·v_wg) divided by the working gas volume in MWh. Everything that raises the booked rates without raising the cycled volume pushes the break-even price up.

prompt: Explain material, immaterial and institutional infrastructure.
solution:
Jochimsen's classification, which the lecture follows, splits infrastructure into three types:

Material infrastructure — the totality of all facilities, equipment and resources of an economy that serve energy supply, transport and telecommunications, i.e. the physical capital stock. Pipelines, power lines, substations, storage caverns, roads, ports, LNG terminals.

Institutional infrastructure — the evolved and established norms, institutions and procedures within which economic activity takes place: the legal framework, property rights, the regulatory authorities, standards and the market rules. In our field: the Energiewirtschaftsgesetz, the EU directives, the Bundesnetzagentur, unbundling rules, DVGW standards, the entry-exit market model.

Immaterial infrastructure — the number and characteristics of the individuals in the division of labour, with regard to their ability to contribute to the level and degree of integration of economic activity. In plain terms: human capital — education, qualification, know-how, health, mobility and willingness to work.

The point of the classification is that infrastructure is not only steel in the ground. A pipeline without a legal access regime and without engineers who can operate it produces nothing.

prompt: Assign five examples to the three categories of infrastructure.
solution:
Material infrastructure: a natural gas transmission pipeline; a 380 kV overhead line; an underground gas storage cavern; an LNG import terminal; a compressor station.

Institutional infrastructure: the Energiewirtschaftsgesetz (EnWG); the Bundesnetzagentur as regulatory authority; the unbundling rules of the EU internal market directives; the entry-exit market model and its capacity booking platform (PRISMA); the DVGW gas quality standards.

Immaterial infrastructure: the qualification of engineers and dispatchers who run the grid; the training and education system that produces them; the know-how of the operators; the health and mobility of the workforce; the willingness to cooperate across companies.

The safe way to sort an example: if you can trip over it, it is material. If it is a rule, a law or a body, it is institutional. If it sits in people's heads, it is immaterial.

prompt: Calculate the cost of reserving transport capacity for one year under an entry-exit pricing system.
solution:
In an entry-exit system the shipper books capacity at an entry point and, independently, at an exit point; there is no route and no distance in the tariff. Total cost = entry price · booked entry capacity + exit price · booked exit capacity, each converted to energy first.

κ_E = κ_V · GCV
C_TE = κ_E · p_Entry + κ_E · p_Exit · 365 (whenever the exit price is quoted per day)

Lecture example (slide 199): κ_V = 10,000 m³/h, GCV = 11 kWh/m³, p_Entry = 1.7 €/kWh/h/a, p_Exit = 0.00219178 €/kWh/h/d
κ_E = 10,000 · 11 = 110,000 kWh/h
C_TE = 110,000 · 1.7 + 110,000 · 365 · 0.00219178 = 187,000 + 88,000 = 275,000 €/a

The exam variant (slide 229) uses p_Entry = 2 €/kWh/h/a and p_Exit = 0.01 €/kWh/h/d:
Entry = 110,000 kW · 2 €/kW/a = 220,000 €/a
Exit = 110,000 kW · 0.01 €/kW/d · 365 d/a = 401,500 €/a
Total = 621,500 €/a

Two traps: convert m³/h into kWh/h before anything else, and check whether the price is per year or per day — the exit price usually is per day and has to be multiplied by 365. Contrast this with distance-related pricing (price · distance · capacity) and postage stamp pricing (price · capacity, one flat tariff for the whole network); entry-exit is the system that removes "pancaking" across several networks.

prompt: What is incentive-based regulation, and what is price-cap regulation?
solution:
The lecture splits regulatory procedures into two families:

Cost-based regulation — rate-of-return and cost-plus. The allowed revenue is derived from the company's own costs, so the regulated firm is reimbursed for what it spends.

Incentive-based regulation — price cap, revenue cap and yardstick competition. The allowed price or revenue is set in advance and decoupled from actual costs, so every euro the company saves stays with it. That is the incentive: cost reduction becomes profitable instead of pointless.

Price-cap regulation sets a ceiling for the price of the regulated service over a regulatory period, usually with an RPI − X formula: the cap may rise with inflation but must fall by a productivity factor X each year. Advantages: strong incentive for efficiency, low information requirement for the regulator, no direct cost audit. Problems: the quality of service can be cut to save money, so quality regulation has to be added; the company may earn very high profits if X was set too low, which is politically hard to defend and may be answered with a profit-sharing factor — but that in turn reduces the incentive for cost reduction.

Revenue cap works the same way on total revenue instead of price, which removes the incentive to sell more volume. Yardstick competition benchmarks each company against the others and gives continuous incentives, but assumes timely implementation and invites coordination between the regulated firms.

prompt: What is the Averch-Johnson effect, and in which context does it belong?
solution:
Context: it is the classic weakness of rate-of-return regulation, i.e. of cost-based regulation — the opposite family to the incentive-based procedures.

Under rate-of-return regulation the company may earn a fixed permitted return on its invested capital. The company therefore maximises profit subject to an upper limit on the return on capital. Since profit is a percentage of the capital base, the way to earn more is to make the capital base larger: the firm over-invests, uses excessive capital and distorts the factor mix towards capital and away from labour and operating expenditure. That systematic gold-plating is the Averch-Johnson effect.

The lecture lists it together with the other issues of rate-of-return regulation: no incentive for a more efficient factor allocation or for reducing operating costs, and information and control problems in implementation — the regulator can hardly tell a necessary investment from an unnecessary one.

The answer to it is incentive-based regulation: decouple the allowed revenue from the company's own costs (price cap, revenue cap, yardstick competition), so that neither over-investment nor inflated operating costs pay off.

prompt: The lecture lists the economic characteristics of infrastructure. Pick two of them and explain them.
solution:
The slide lists five: large investment projects with high capital requirements, external effects, economies of scale, step costs, and a high proportion of fixed costs. Two worth explaining:

Economies of scale. The average cost per transported unit falls as output grows, because the huge fixed cost of the asset is spread over more units and because the physics helps: the capacity of a pipe grows faster than its surface, so a larger diameter carries disproportionately more gas for the same metre of steel. This is what makes the grid a natural monopoly — one large operator is cheaper than two small ones — and is therefore the economic root of regulation.

Step costs. Capacity cannot be added continuously. You can build a 30-inch or a 36-inch pipeline, not a 33.7-inch one; a compressor comes in discrete sizes. Investment therefore comes in lumps, capacity jumps ahead of demand, and the new asset is under-utilised for years until demand grows into it. That is why infrastructure planning always argues over long horizons and why utilisation figures matter so much.

The other three, briefly: high capital requirements make financing and long amortisation periods a defining feature; external effects mean benefits and costs fall on third parties, which markets do not price; the high fixed-cost share means marginal cost pricing does not cover total cost, so a capacity charge is needed.

prompt: Name and explain the three functions of natural gas storage.
solution:
1. Compensation of demand fluctuations — short-term and mid-term. Gas demand is strongly temperature-correlated: households and heating consume several times more in January than in July, and within a day there are morning and evening peaks. Production and pipeline imports, by contrast, run close to a flat band because their capacity is expensive and wants high utilisation. Storage takes the difference: it is filled in summer and emptied in winter (seasonal, mid-term) and it covers the daily and hourly peaks (short-term, peak shaving).

2. Compensation of supply fluctuations. If a producing field, a pipeline or an LNG cargo fails, the storage steps in. This is the security-of-supply function that the EU and German storage laws turned into a legal filling obligation after 2022 — storage substitutes for supply that does not arrive.

3. (Economic) optimisation. Storage is also a trading asset. Gas is bought when it is cheap and sold when it is expensive; the condition is p_supply + p_storage < p_sales. On top of that the store can be re-optimised as prices move, which is where the option value of a storage booking comes from.

The three functions correspond to three different technical profiles: seasonal stores (depleted fields, aquifers — large working gas volume, low rates) serve function 1 and 2, salt caverns (small volume, high rates, several cycles per year) serve the peak and the trading function.

prompt: Draw the LNG value chain and say which steps cause the highest costs.
solution:
The chain, left to right, five stages:

1. Exploration & production — find the field, produce and treat the gas.
2. Refrigeration & liquefaction — remove CO2, water, H2S and heavy hydrocarbons, then cool to about −162 °C. The volume shrinks by roughly a factor of 600. This is the liquefaction train, the capital-intensive heart of the chain.
3. Transportation — loading and shipping in LNG carriers (Moss spherical or membrane tanks), with boil-off gas used as fuel.
4. Storage & regasification — the import terminal: LNG tanks, vaporisers, feed-in into the receiving grid.
5. Customer.

Cost breakdown from the lecture's slide: exploration and production 11 %, refrigeration and liquefaction 42 %, transportation 20 %, storage and regasification 27 %.

So the answer to the second half: liquefaction is by far the most expensive step at 42 %, followed by storage and regasification at 27 %. The sea leg itself, at 20 %, is comparatively cheap — and that is exactly why LNG beats pipelines over long distances: the expensive parts sit at the two ends and do not grow with distance.

prompt: Using a sketch, explain what compressor stations are needed for.
solution:
Sketch: pressure on the vertical axis, distance along the pipeline on the horizontal axis. The pressure falls along the line because of friction — a sawtooth: it drops steadily, then jumps back up at each compressor station, drops again, and so on. Mark the minimum pressure the line must not fall below and the maximum design pressure.

What compressors do: they maintain the pressure. Gas flows only along a pressure gradient, and friction eats that gradient, so without re-compression the throughput would collapse after a few hundred kilometres. Lecture figures: pipelines up to 6,000 km long, diameter up to 1,400 mm, pressure up to 100 bar, compressor spacing 80 to 500 km, driven by natural gas or electricity, consuming up to about 0.5 % of the throughput per 100 km.

The economics: transport capacity can be bought either with more steel (a larger diameter) or with more compression (more stations). Both cost money, so the design is an economic compromise between the number of compressors and the pipeline diameter — the optimisation slide shows the same capacity realised as 44″ with few stations or 34″ with many. The cost of the energy for compression can dominate the trade-off. Compressors are also needed at storage facilities to inject gas against reservoir pressure.

prompt: Name the four chemical reaction equations: Haber-Bosch, water-gas shift, electrolysis and steam reforming.
solution:
Steam reforming (SMR): CH4 + H2O → CO + 3 H2
Endothermic; the reaction heat comes from burning methane and part of the hydrogen with air, which also supplies the nitrogen for the ammonia synthesis. This is step 1 of conventional (grey) ammonia and the dominant route to hydrogen today.

Water-gas shift: CO + H2O → CO2 + H2
The carbon monoxide is reacted with further steam to raise the hydrogen yield. If the CO2 is captured here, the product is called blue hydrogen or blue ammonia.

Water electrolysis: 2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2
The renewable route. Alkaline about 4.7 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 64 % efficiency), SOEC about 3.6 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 83 %).

Haber-Bosch: N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3, ΔH° = −91.8 kJ/mol
At 400–450 °C and 120–220 bar over an iron catalyst; exothermic, but energy is needed for compression and pre-heating. Conversion per pass is below 20 %, limited by thermodynamics, so the ammonia is condensed out and the unreacted gas is recycled. Stoichiometrically 1 kg NH3 needs 0.18 kg H2 and 0.82 kg N2.

Sequence to remember: 1–2 make grey hydrogen from methane, 3 makes green hydrogen from water and power, 4 turns hydrogen into ammonia either way.

prompt: For hydrogen, ammonia and methanol: in which transport and storage options can existing infrastructure be re-used — ship, pipeline, underground storage?
solution:
From the comparison table of H2 derivatives:

Hydrogen. Ship: no re-use — there is only one prototype carrier of 2,200 dwt. Pipeline: re-use possible, repurposing existing natural gas pipelines costs 10–35 % of new construction. Underground storage: possible in salt caverns, which is the storage option the lecture discusses; porous formations are far less proven for hydrogen. Storage in tanks needs refrigeration or high pressure.

Ammonia. Ship: established, ships up to 75,000 dwt, and 126 ammonia terminals already exist; LPG carriers can be re-used. Pipeline: no re-use of gas pipelines. Storage: refrigerated or pressure tanks; established practice from the fertiliser industry.

Methanol. Ship: established, with potential re-use of oil tankers — the table gives no size limit in the methanol column; the "> 500,000 dwt" figure belongs to LOHCs and Fischer-Tropsch fuels. Pipeline: compatibility unclear. Storage: high compatibility — liquid at ambient conditions, so ordinary product tanks work.

The pattern behind the table: the more a molecule behaves like an existing fuel, the more infrastructure it inherits. Methanol and Fischer-Tropsch fuels inherit the oil world, SNG inherits the entire natural gas world, ammonia inherits the LPG and fertiliser world — and pure hydrogen inherits almost nothing and has to be built from scratch.

prompt: How much hydrogen is consumed worldwide today, and roughly how much will be consumed around the middle of the century?
solution:
Today: global hydrogen production and consumption is about 110 Mt per year, of which renewable hydrogen is less than 1 % — roughly 0.09 Mt/a. It is almost entirely used as a chemical feedstock, not as an energy carrier: ammonia and fertiliser production takes about 45 % of it, refining most of the rest, plus methanol and steel.

2050: the projections in the lecture run in the range of roughly 500–700 Mt per year, i.e. a five- to sixfold increase, with the new demand coming from sectors that do not use hydrogen today — steel via direct reduction, shipping and aviation fuels, high-temperature industrial heat and some power generation.

Two caveats the lecture insists on. First, the projections diverge enormously between sources and have been revised downwards repeatedly — the slide on the uncertainty in global hydrogen trade projections is there for exactly that reason. Second, the clean hydrogen ladder ranks the applications: hydrogen is unavoidable for fertiliser, refining and steel, and a poor choice for domestic heating and passenger cars, where direct electrification wins.
note: Give the 110 Mt/a and the < 1 % renewable share as the hard numbers — those are printed on the slide. The 2050 figure depends on the source shown (IEA, IRENA, Hydrogen Council), so quote it as a range and say which scenario you mean.

prompt: How much electrolyser capacity is installed worldwide, and how much would be needed?
solution:
Installed: about 2 GW of electrolysis capacity worldwide by the end of 2024, with almost 5 GW expected by the end of 2025.

Needed: about 5,000 GW by 2050 — three orders of magnitude more than what stands today.

Put next to the 110 Mt/a of hydrogen produced today of which less than 1 % is renewable, this is the central reality check of the whole lecture: the announced projects and the physical build-out are far apart. The European roadmap on the following slide makes the same point in phases — phase 1 (2020–2024) 6 GW and more than 1 Mt/a, phase 2 (2025–2030) 40 GW and more than 10 Mt/a plus more than 10 Mt/a of imports.

If you are asked for one sentence: roughly 2 GW installed against roughly 5,000 GW required, so today's capacity is about 0.04 % of what the 2050 scenarios assume.

prompt: The consumption of an alkaline electrolyser, the efficiency of the liquefaction plant and the daily consumption of the ship are given. Determine the overall efficiency of transporting hydrogen over 10 days.
solution:
Work through the chain step by step and multiply the efficiencies; the exercise sheet does exactly this for a 20-day voyage.

1. Electrolysis. Alkaline needs 4.7 kWh/Nm³. With a density of 0.0899 kg/Nm³ that is 4.7 / 0.0899 = 52.28 kWh_el per kg H2. Against the lower heating value of 33.33 kWh/kg the efficiency is 33.33 / 52.28 = 63.8 %.

2. Liquefaction. 7 kWh_el per kg H2 on top. For 1 MWh of electricity available for electrolysis and liquefaction combined:
1,000 kWh / (52.28 + 7) kWh/kg = 16.87 kg H2, containing 16.87 · 33.33 = 562.2 kWh.
Efficiency up to the ship: 562.2 / 1,000 = 56.2 %.

3. Voyage. Liquid hydrogen boils off continuously at 0.2 % per day. After 10 days:
16.87 kg · 0.998^10 = 16.54 kg, i.e. 551.3 kWh.
(The sheet's 20-day case gives 16.87 · 0.998^20 = 16.21 kg / 540.2 kWh.)

Overall efficiency over 10 days = 551.3 / 1,000 = 55.1 %.

The comparison the exercise is really after: the same 1 MWh routed through electrolysis, air separation and Haber-Bosch yields 100.95 kg of ammonia with 521.9 kWh, and ammonia has no boil-off problem. Hydrogen starts ahead and loses its lead the longer the voyage lasts.
note: The lecturer's own solution sheet writes "1,000 MWh_el" in the ammonia step — it has to be 1,000 kWh_el, otherwise the result of 100.95 kg NH3 does not follow. Use kWh throughout.

prompt: Given the cost data of a CCGT and a coal-fired plant: at which CO2 price do both have the same variable costs?
solution:
Write the variable generation cost of each plant as a straight line in the CO2 price p:

c_var = (fuel + logistic costs per MWh_th) / η + (specific CO2 emissions per MWh_th / η) · p + auxiliary costs

With the exercise data:
Hard coal — efficiency η = 40 %, fuel + logistics 12.24 €/MWh_th, 0.35 tCO2/MWh_th, auxiliary 0.65 €/MWh_el:
c_coal = 12.24/0.40 + (0.35/0.40)·p + 0.65 = 31.25 + 0.875·p
CCGT — η = 53 %, fuel + logistics 29.15 €/MWh_th, 0.184 tCO2/MWh_th, auxiliary 1.53 €/MWh_el:
c_CCGT = 29.15/0.53 + (0.184/0.53)·p + 1.53 = 56.52 + 0.3472·p

Check at the exercise's own CO2 price of 10 €/t: coal 40.00 €/MWh_el, CCGT 60.00 €/MWh_el — exactly the figures used in the dispatch exercise.

Set them equal:
31.25 + 0.875·p = 56.52 + 0.3472·p
0.5278·p = 25.27
p ≈ 47.9 €/tCO2

Above roughly 48 €/t the gas plant becomes cheaper than hard coal and the two swap places in the merit order — the fuel switch. For completeness with the same data set: lignite overtakes CCGT at about 52 €/t and hard coal at about 66 €/t.

The mechanism to state in words: the CO2 price hits the dirtier plant harder because its emission factor per MWh_el is larger, so raising it rotates the merit order.

prompt: An island has three 200 MW power plants with given marginal costs. The load is 600 MW for 1,500 h/a, 400 MW for 3,000 h/a and 200 MW for the rest of the year. Uncovered demand has to be imported over an external line at 300 €/MWh for the first 600 MW, 200 €/MWh for 400 MW and 100 €/MWh for 200 MW. What does covering the uncovered demand cost, and what does the operator earn with the three plants?
solution:
Method — this is the load-duration-curve version of the dispatch exercise.

Step 1: build the load duration curve as steps. 600 MW for 1,500 h, 400 MW for the next 3,000 h, 200 MW for the remaining 8,760 − 1,500 − 3,000 = 4,260 h.
Energy = 600·1,500 + 400·3,000 + 200·4,260 = 900,000 + 1,200,000 + 852,000 = 2,952,000 MWh/a.

Step 2: import cost if nothing is covered locally. Multiply each block by its own import price:
600 MW · 1,500 h · 300 €/MWh = 270,000,000 €
400 MW · 3,000 h · 200 €/MWh = 240,000,000 €
200 MW · 4,260 h · 100 €/MWh = 85,200,000 €
Total ≈ 595.2 million €/a.

Step 3: dispatch the local plants by merit order. Sort the three 200 MW units by marginal cost and run the cheapest first, for as many hours as the load duration curve is above the corresponding capacity band. Any block whose local marginal cost lies below the import price of that block is served locally; the rest stays on the line.

Step 4: the operator's earnings. In each block the price is set by the marginal unit — here the import price, because the line is the expensive marginal supplier. Contribution margin = (import price of the block − own marginal cost) · own energy in that block. Sum over the blocks. The cheap base-load unit earns in every hour it runs, the expensive unit earns only in the 1,500 peak hours.

What the examiner wants to see: the load duration curve drawn in steps, the merit order applied to it, energy = capacity · hours for each block, and the margin computed as price minus marginal cost, not as revenue.
note: The memory protocol only recalls this task roughly and does not record the plants' marginal costs ("or something like that"). The method above is the one the exercise uses; plug in whatever marginal costs the exam sheet gives.

prompt: Label the figure "Selected planning tasks of utilities" completely.
solution:
The figure has three time bands on the left, each split into a physical and a trading column, and two axes on the right.

Time horizons (left column): online — < 1 a — 1–5 a — > 5 a.

Short-term planning (< 1 a):
 physical world: day-ahead planning / unit commitment; real-time balancing (on behalf of the TSO), which is the "online" row
 trading: day-ahead trading; intraday trading

Mid-term planning (1–5 a):
 physical world: portfolio optimisation; maintenance planning
 trading: future and forward trading; hedging / risk management

Long-term (strategic) planning (> 5 a):
 physical world: investment / expansion; disinvestment / decommissioning
 trading: structured products / "virtual power plants"

Column headings: "Physical world" on the left, "Financial and physical trading activities" on the right.

Right-hand axes: a wedge labelled increasing uncertainty, running from deterministic at the bottom to increasing uncertainty at the top; alongside it the methods that match each horizon — deterministic optimisation for the short term, stochastic approaches for the mid term, scenario planning for the long term.

The message of the figure: the further out you plan, the less you know, and the method has to change with the horizon — which is why the lecture pairs energy systems analysis with scenario planning.

prompt: Perfect foresight versus time-step approach: give two characteristics and one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
solution:
Perfect foresight
 Characteristics: all input assumptions over the whole calculation horizon are known to the model from the start; the model optimises all periods simultaneously in one problem, so an investment in 2030 can already anticipate the CO2 price of 2045.
 Advantage: the result is the true system optimum over the horizon — consistent, path-optimal and the correct benchmark for what an ideal planner would do.
 Disadvantage: it is unrealistic. No real investor knows the next 30 years; the model therefore systematically avoids mistakes that real actors make, understates stranded assets and tends to underestimate cost.

Time-step approach
 Characteristics: only the assumptions of the individual time step are known to the expansion decision; the model is solved step by step and each step inherits the capacity stock the previous step left behind.
 Advantage: much closer to real decision behaviour under limited information, and it can reproduce misinvestment, lock-in and stranded assets — the phenomena that actually occur.
 Disadvantage: the result is path-dependent and generally not the global optimum; decisions made early cannot be revised, so the outcome depends on how the steps are cut.

One-liner: perfect foresight answers "what would be optimal?", the time-step approach answers "what would plausibly happen?".

prompt: You own one power plant with high marginal costs and one with low marginal costs. Which would you deploy in Germany and why? How would your decision look in Italy?
solution:
The rule first. Under the merit order principle every producer bids its variable production costs, the plants are called cheapest first, and the marginal plant in each hour sets the price. So the decision is not about the plant in isolation but about where its marginal costs sit in the national merit order — that is what determines the number of hours it runs and the margin it earns.

Germany. The merit order is long and starts low: a large nuclear and lignite base historically, plenty of hard coal, and a very large share of renewables with marginal costs near zero that pushes the residual load down. A plant with low marginal costs is therefore in the money for many hours and would be the one to run. A plant with high marginal costs — a gas peaker — is only called in the few hours of high residual load; it needs high price spreads rather than many full-load hours, and it earns most of its money in scarcity hours.

Italy. The generation mix is dominated by gas, imports and hydro; there is hardly any coal or lignite left, so the merit order sits at a higher level and the wholesale price is structurally higher than in Germany. A plant whose marginal costs count as "high" in Germany can be mid-merit or even in-merit in Italy and would run far more hours there. The same asset therefore has a completely different value depending on which merit order it is placed in.

Answer in one sentence: deploy the low-marginal-cost plant wherever it is available, because the merit order calls the cheapest capacity first — but the label "high marginal costs" is relative to the national merit order, and a plant that is a peaker in Germany can be a base-load plant in Italy.
